title: Spaghetti Carbonara
shortDescription: Classic Roman pasta with guanciale, eggs, and Pecorino Romano
note: Work quickly off heat to prevent scrambling the eggs
pairingSuggestion: Pairs well with a crisp Frascati or other dry white wine.
introCopy: This iconic Roman dish relies on just a handful of ingredients and perfect timing. The silky sauce comes from tempering eggs with pasta water, not cream—a common misconception. Use guanciale if possible, though pancetta works in a pinch.

steps.text: Bring a large pot of salted water to boil. Cook spaghetti until al dente, reserving 1 cup pasta water before draining.
Meanwhile, cook guanciale in a large skillet over medium heat until crispy and fat is rendered, about 8 minutes. Remove from heat.
In a bowl, whisk together egg yolks, whole eggs, Pecorino, and black pepper until smooth.
Add hot drained pasta to the skillet with guanciale. Toss to coat in the fat.
Remove skillet from heat completely. Add egg mixture and toss vigorously, adding reserved pasta water a little at a time until sauce is creamy and coats the pasta. Serve immediately.

title: Bucatini all'Amatriciana
shortDescription: Spicy tomato sauce with guanciale and Pecorino
note: Guanciale's rendered fat is essential to this dish
introCopy: Named after the town of Amatrice, this robust pasta dish features a tomato sauce enriched with crispy guanciale and a kick from red pepper flakes. The hollow bucatini pasta soaks up the flavorful sauce beautifully.

steps.text: Cook guanciale in a large skillet over medium heat until crispy and fat is rendered, about 8 minutes.
Add red pepper flakes and cook for 30 seconds. Add wine and let it evaporate.
Add crushed tomatoes and simmer for 15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until sauce thickens.
Meanwhile, cook bucatini in salted boiling water until al dente. Reserve 1 cup pasta water before draining.
Add drained pasta to sauce with a splash of pasta water. Toss to combine. Remove from heat, add half the Pecorino, and toss again. Serve with remaining cheese.

title: Penne all'Arrabbiata
shortDescription: Fiery tomato sauce with garlic and red chili
note: Adjust chili to your heat preference
introCopy: Arrabbiata means 'angry' in Italian, referring to the heat from generous amounts of red chili. This simple yet bold sauce comes together quickly, making it perfect for weeknight dinners when you want something with a kick.

steps.text: Heat olive oil in a large skillet over medium heat. Add garlic and red pepper flakes, cook until garlic is golden, about 2 minutes.
Add crushed tomatoes and salt. Simmer for 15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until sauce thickens.
Meanwhile, cook penne in salted boiling water until al dente. Reserve 1/2 cup pasta water before draining.
Add drained pasta to sauce with a splash of pasta water. Toss to coat. Stir in parsley and serve immediately.

title: Tagliatelle Bolognese
shortDescription: Rich meat ragù from Bologna with fresh egg pasta
note: Low and slow is the secret to deep flavor
pairingSuggestion: Pairs well with a medium-bodied Sangiovese.
introCopy: Authentic ragù Bolognese is a labor of love, simmered for hours until the meat becomes meltingly tender and the sauce deeply concentrated. Traditionally served with fresh tagliatelle, never spaghetti, this is Sunday cooking at its finest.

steps.text: Heat olive oil in a large heavy pot over medium heat. Add pancetta and cook until fat renders, about 5 minutes.
Add onion, carrot, and celery. Cook until softened, about 10 minutes.
Add ground beef and pork. Cook, breaking up with a spoon, until browned, about 10 minutes.
Add wine and simmer until evaporated, about 5 minutes.
Add milk and simmer until absorbed, about 10 minutes. Add nutmeg.
Add crushed tomatoes, tomato paste, and stock. Season with salt and pepper. Bring to a simmer.
Reduce heat to very low. Simmer gently, partially covered, for 2.5-3 hours, stirring occasionally and adding water if needed to maintain a thick but saucy consistency.
When ragù is nearly done, cook tagliatelle in salted boiling water until al dente, 2-3 minutes for fresh pasta.
Toss drained pasta with ragù. Serve topped with Parmigiano-Reggiano.

title: Linguine alle Vongole
shortDescription: Linguine with clams in white wine and garlic
note: Purge clams in salt water before cooking
introCopy: This elegant seafood pasta is a staple along Italy's coastline. Fresh clams release their briny juices into garlicky white wine, creating a light yet flavorful sauce that needs nothing more than good olive oil and a handful of parsley.

steps.text: Cook linguine in salted boiling water until just shy of al dente. Reserve 1 cup pasta water before draining.
Meanwhile, heat olive oil in a large skillet over medium heat. Add garlic and red pepper flakes, cook until fragrant, about 1 minute.
Add wine and bring to a simmer. Add clams, cover, and cook until clams open, 5-7 minutes. Discard any unopened clams.
Add drained pasta and parsley to skillet. Toss with clams and sauce, adding pasta water as needed to create a silky sauce. Serve immediately.

title: Trofie al Pesto Genovese
shortDescription: Twisted pasta with basil pesto, potatoes, and green beans
note: Never heat pesto—toss with hot pasta off the heat
introCopy: From Liguria comes this vibrant green sauce made by pounding fresh basil, pine nuts, garlic, and cheese. Traditionally served with trofie, small twisted pasta, along with boiled potatoes and green beans for a complete meal.

steps.text: Make pesto: In a food processor, combine basil, pine nuts, and garlic. Pulse until finely chopped. Add cheeses and pulse to combine. With motor running, drizzle in olive oil until smooth. Season with salt.
Bring a large pot of salted water to boil. Add potatoes and cook for 5 minutes.

Add pasta to the pot with potatoes. After 5 minutes, add green beans. Continue cooking until pasta is al dente and vegetables are tender, about 5 more minutes. Reserve 1 cup pasta water before draining.
Transfer drained pasta and vegetables to a large bowl. Add pesto and toss, adding pasta water a little at a time until sauce coats everything nicely. Serve immediately with extra cheese if desired.

title: Potato Gnocchi with Butter and Sage
shortDescription: Pillowy potato dumplings in brown butter with crispy sage
note: Use starchy potatoes and work quickly while they're hot
introCopy: Light-as-air gnocchi are surprisingly simple to make at home. The key is using the right potatoes and handling the dough gently. Tossed in nutty brown butter with crispy sage leaves, this is comfort food at its most elegant.

steps.text: Boil whole unpeeled potatoes until tender, about 30 minutes. Drain and let cool slightly, then peel while still warm.
Pass potatoes through a ricer onto a clean work surface. Make a well in the center and add flour, egg, and salt. Gently knead until just combined—don't overwork.
Divide dough into 6 pieces. Roll each into a 3/4-inch thick rope. Cut into 1-inch pieces. Roll each piece down a gnocchi board or fork to create ridges. Place on a floured baking sheet.
Bring a large pot of salted water to a gentle boil. Cook gnocchi in batches—they're done when they float to the surface, about 2 minutes. Remove with a slotted spoon.
Meanwhile, melt butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add sage leaves and cook until butter is golden brown and sage is crispy, 3-4 minutes.
Add cooked gnocchi to the butter and toss gently to coat. Serve immediately with Parmigiano-Reggiano.

title: Rigatoni alla Puttanesca
shortDescription: Bold tomato sauce with olives, capers, and anchovies
note: The anchovies dissolve into savory depth
introCopy: This punchy Neapolitan sauce comes together in the time it takes to boil pasta. Salty olives and capers, briny anchovies, and sweet tomatoes create a complex flavor that belies the dish's simplicity. Legend says it was invented by working women who needed something quick between clients.

steps.text: Heat olive oil in a large skillet over medium heat. Add anchovies and cook, stirring, until dissolved, about 2 minutes.
Add garlic and red pepper flakes. Cook until fragrant, about 1 minute.
Add crushed tomatoes, olives, and capers. Simmer for 15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until sauce thickens.
Meanwhile, cook rigatoni in salted boiling water until al dente. Reserve 1/2 cup pasta water before draining.
Add drained pasta to sauce with a splash of pasta water. Toss to coat. Stir in parsley and serve immediately.

title: Saltimbocca alla Romana
shortDescription: Veal cutlets with prosciutto and sage in white wine sauce
note: Saltimbocca means 'jumps in the mouth' for good reason
introCopy: This Roman classic is all about quality ingredients prepared simply. Tender veal is topped with salty prosciutto and fresh sage, then quickly pan-fried and finished with white wine and butter. It comes together in minutes but tastes like you've been cooking all day.

steps.text: Place one slice of prosciutto on each veal cutlet. Top with 2 sage leaves. Secure with a toothpick through the center.
Season cutlets with salt and pepper, then lightly dredge in flour, shaking off excess.

Heat olive oil and 1 tablespoon butter in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Cook cutlets prosciutto-side down first, until golden, about 2 minutes. Flip and cook 1-2 minutes more. Work in batches if needed. Transfer to a platter and keep warm.
Add wine to the skillet and scrape up browned bits. Simmer until reduced by half, about 2 minutes.
Remove from heat and swirl in remaining 2 tablespoons butter. Pour sauce over cutlets and serve immediately.

title: Polenta Cremosa
shortDescription: Creamy cornmeal porridge with butter and Parmesan
note: Stir constantly for the creamiest texture
introCopy: Soft polenta is northern Italy's answer to mashed potatoes. When made properly with plenty of stirring, it becomes luxuriously creamy. Enriched with butter and Parmesan, it's the perfect bed for braised meats, mushrooms, or rich ragùs.

steps.text: Bring water and salt to a boil in a large heavy pot. Reduce heat to medium-low.
Add polenta in a slow, steady stream, whisking constantly to prevent lumps.
Switch to a wooden spoon and cook, stirring frequently, until polenta is thick and creamy and no longer gritty, 35-40 minutes. If it becomes too thick, add hot water a little at a time.
Remove from heat. Stir in butter and Parmigiano-Reggiano until melted and incorporated. Season with black pepper. Serve immediately.

title: Insalata Caprese
shortDescription: Tomato, mozzarella, and basil salad with olive oil
note: Use only the ripest tomatoes and freshest mozzarella
introCopy: This iconic salad from the island of Capri celebrates the colors of the Italian flag. With just a few ingredients, quality is everything—seek out ripe heirloom tomatoes, creamy buffalo mozzarella, and peppery fresh basil. A drizzle of excellent olive oil brings it all together.

steps.text: Arrange tomato and mozzarella slices on a platter, alternating and slightly overlapping them.
Tuck basil leaves between the slices.
Drizzle generously with olive oil and sprinkle with sea salt and black pepper. If using, drizzle with balsamic vinegar. Serve immediately at room temperature.

title: Bruschetta al Pomodoro
shortDescription: Grilled bread with marinated tomatoes and basil
note: The bread should be crunchy outside, soft inside
introCopy: This quintessential Italian appetizer is all about contrast—crunchy grilled bread rubbed with garlic meets juicy marinated tomatoes. It's summer on a plate, best made when tomatoes are at their peak. The key is letting the tomatoes sit to develop flavor.

steps.text: Combine diced tomatoes, minced garlic, basil, 3 tablespoons olive oil, and balsamic vinegar in a bowl. Season with salt and pepper. Let sit for 15 minutes to meld flavors.
Meanwhile, brush bread slices with remaining olive oil. Grill or toast until golden and crispy, about 2 minutes per side.
While still warm, rub one side of each bread slice with the whole garlic clove.
Top each slice with tomato mixture and serve immediately.

title: Arancini al Ragù
shortDescription: Sicilian fried rice balls with meat sauce and mozzarella
note: Day-old risotto works best for shaping
introCopy: These golden fried rice balls are a Sicilian street food treasure. Creamy risotto is stuffed with ragù and mozzarella, breaded, and fried until crispy. Though they take some effort, they're perfect for using up leftover risotto and can be made ahead and frozen.

steps.text: Make risotto: Sauté rice briefly, then add stock one ladle at a time, stirring frequently, until rice is al dente and creamy, about 18 minutes. Stir in Parmigiano, saffron if using, and let cool. When cool, stir in 2 beaten eggs. Refrigerate until firm, at least 2 hours or overnight.
With damp hands, take about 3 tablespoons of risotto and form into a ball. Make an indentation in the center.
Fill with about 1 teaspoon ragù and a small cube of mozzarella. Cover with more risotto and roll into a smooth ball. Repeat with remaining ingredients.
Set up breading station: flour, beaten eggs, and breadcrumbs in separate shallow bowls. Roll each ball in flour, then egg, then breadcrumbs, ensuring complete coverage.
Heat oil to 350°F (175°C) in a deep pot. Fry arancini in batches, turning occasionally, until deep golden brown, about 4-5 minutes. Drain on paper towels.
Let cool for 5 minutes before serving—the inside will be very hot.

title: Lasagne alla Bolognese
shortDescription: Layers of pasta, ragù, and béchamel baked until golden
note: Let it rest 15 minutes before slicing for clean cuts
introCopy: This is the real lasagna—from Bologna, not Italy-via-America. Thin sheets of fresh pasta are layered with rich meat ragù and creamy béchamel (no ricotta in sight). It's an investment of time that pays dividends in pure comfort.

steps.text: Make béchamel: Heat milk until steaming. In a separate pot, melt butter over medium heat. Whisk in flour and cook, stirring, for 2 minutes. Gradually whisk in hot milk. Cook, stirring constantly, until thick enough to coat a spoon, about 10 minutes. Season with nutmeg and salt. Set aside.
Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Butter a 9x13-inch baking dish.
Spread a thin layer of béchamel on the bottom of the dish. Top with a layer of pasta sheets (cut to fit if needed).
Spread a layer of ragù, then béchamel, then sprinkle with Parmigiano. Repeat layers, ending with béchamel and a generous topping of Parmigiano. Dot with butter.
Cover with foil and bake for 30 minutes. Remove foil and bake until golden and bubbling, about 20 more minutes.
Let rest for 15 minutes before slicing and serving.

title: Pollo alla Cacciatore
shortDescription: Hunter-style chicken braised with tomatoes and peppers
note: Browning the chicken first builds flavor in the sauce
introCopy: Cacciatore means 'hunter' in Italian, and this rustic dish has as many variations as there are hunters. Chicken is browned, then braised with tomatoes, bell peppers, and aromatics until fall-off-the-bone tender. Serve over polenta or with crusty bread to soak up the sauce.

steps.text: Season chicken pieces generously with salt and pepper.
Heat olive oil in a large Dutch oven over medium-high heat. Brown chicken in batches until golden on all sides, about 10 minutes total. Remove and set aside.
Add onion and peppers to the pot. Cook until softened, about 8 minutes. Add mushrooms and cook until they release their liquid, about 5 minutes.
Add garlic and cook for 1 minute. Add wine and scrape up browned bits. Let reduce for 2 minutes.
Add tomatoes, stock, rosemary, and bay leaves. Return chicken to pot, nestling into the sauce. Bring to a simmer.
Cover and simmer gently until chicken is very tender, about 40 minutes.
Remove bay leaves and rosemary sprigs. Adjust seasoning. Sprinkle with parsley and serve.

title: Chicken Milanese
shortDescription: Breaded chicken cutlets with arugula and lemon
note: Pound the chicken thin for even cooking
introCopy: This northern Italian classic features thin chicken cutlets breaded and fried until golden and crispy. Topped with a simple arugula salad dressed in lemon and olive oil, it's elegant enough for company but easy enough for a weeknight.

steps.text: Season chicken with salt and pepper. Set up breading station: flour in one shallow bowl, beaten eggs in another, and breadcrumbs mixed with Parmigiano in a third.
Dredge each chicken breast in flour, shaking off excess. Dip in egg, then coat thoroughly with breadcrumb mixture, pressing to adhere.
Heat olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Fry chicken until golden brown and cooked through, about 3-4 minutes per side. Transfer to a paper towel-lined plate.
Toss arugula with olive oil and lemon juice. Season with salt and pepper.
Top each chicken cutlet with arugula salad. Serve immediately with lemon wedges.

title: Panna Cotta with Berry Compote
shortDescription: Silky vanilla cream dessert with fresh berry sauce
note: Don't over-gelatin or it will be rubbery
introCopy: This elegant northern Italian dessert is deceptively simple—sweetened cream thickened just enough to hold its shape. The name means 'cooked cream,' and when made properly, it should be barely set, trembling on the plate. A tart berry compote provides the perfect contrast.

steps.text: Sprinkle gelatin over cold water in a small bowl. Let stand for 5 minutes to bloom.
Combine cream, sugar, and salt in a saucepan. Heat over medium, stirring, until sugar dissolves and cream just begins to simmer. Remove from heat.
Add bloomed gelatin and vanilla to hot cream, stirring until gelatin completely dissolves.
Pour into 6 ramekins or small bowls. Refrigerate until set, at least 4 hours.
Make compote: Combine berries, sugar, and lemon juice in a small pot. Cook over medium heat until berries break down and sauce thickens slightly, about 8 minutes. Let cool.
To serve, run a knife around the edge of each panna cotta and invert onto plates, or serve in the ramekins. Top with berry compote.

title: Gelato Stracciatella
shortDescription: Creamy vanilla gelato with chocolate shavings
note: Chill the base completely before churning
introCopy: This classic gelato from northern Italy features a rich custard base studded with fine chocolate shavings. The name comes from 'stracciare,' meaning to shred—chocolate is drizzled into the churning gelato and breaks into delicate flakes. It's pure indulgence.

steps.text: Heat milk and cream in a saucepan over medium heat until steaming but not boiling.
Whisk egg yolks, sugar, and salt in a bowl until pale and thick. Gradually whisk in about 1 cup of hot milk to temper the eggs.

Pour egg mixture back into the saucepan. Cook over medium-low heat, stirring constantly with a wooden spoon, until custard thickens and coats the back of the spoon (about 170°F), 8-10 minutes. Do not boil.
Strain custard through a fine-mesh sieve into a clean bowl. Stir in vanilla. Cover and refrigerate until completely cold, at least 4 hours or overnight.
Churn in an ice cream maker according to manufacturer's instructions. In the last minute of churning, drizzle in melted chocolate in a thin stream—it will harden into shavings.
Transfer to a freezer container and freeze until firm, at least 2 hours.

title: Sfogliatelle
shortDescription: Crispy layered pastries filled with ricotta and candied citrus
note: The dough requires patience but results are stunning
introCopy: These shell-shaped Neapolitan pastries are a labor of love. Paper-thin layers of dough are rolled, filled with sweet ricotta, and baked until shattering-crisp. The filling, scented with orange and cinnamon, provides a creamy contrast to the crunchy shell.

steps.text: Make dough: Combine flour and salt. Add water and knead until smooth and elastic, about 10 minutes. Wrap and rest for 30 minutes.
Roll dough as thin as possible into a large rectangle. Spread softened butter evenly over the surface.
Starting from a short end, roll dough into a tight log. Wrap and refrigerate for 1 hour.
Make filling: Mix ricotta, sugar, egg, semolina, candied peel, vanilla, and cinnamon until smooth. Refrigerate.

Cut dough log into 12 equal pieces. Working with one piece at a time (keep others refrigerated), press and stretch with your thumbs from the center outward to create a thin cone shape with layers visible.
Fill each cone with about 2 tablespoons of ricotta filling. Press edges to seal into a clamshell shape.
Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Place pastries on a parchment-lined baking sheet.
Bake until deep golden brown and crispy, 20-25 minutes. Let cool slightly, then dust with powdered sugar.

title: Biscotti di Mandorle
shortDescription: Twice-baked almond cookies perfect for dipping
note: The second bake creates their signature crunch
introCopy: These Tuscan cookies are baked twice to achieve their characteristic dry, crunchy texture. Studded with toasted almonds, they're designed to be dipped in coffee or sweet wine. They keep for weeks in an airtight container, making them perfect for gifting.

steps.text: Preheat oven to 350°F (175°C). Line a baking sheet with parchment.
Whisk together flour, sugar, baking powder, and salt. In another bowl, beat eggs, vanilla, and almond extract.
Add wet ingredients to dry and mix until combined. Fold in toasted almonds.
Divide dough in half. Shape each half into a 12-inch log on the prepared baking sheet, spacing them apart. Flatten slightly.
Bake until golden and firm, about 25 minutes. Let cool for 10 minutes.
Reduce oven to 325°F (165°C). Using a serrated knife, slice logs diagonally into 1/2-inch slices.
Arrange slices cut-side down on baking sheet. Bake for 10 minutes, flip, and bake 10 more minutes until crisp and dry.
Cool completely on a wire rack. Store in an airtight container.

title: Cornetti (Italian Croissants)
shortDescription: Sweet breakfast pastries with a hint of citrus
note: Laminated dough needs patience and cool temperatures
introCopy: Italy's answer to the French croissant, cornetti are slightly sweeter and often scented with vanilla or citrus zest. They're flakier than brioche but softer than a croissant. Enjoyed with cappuccino for breakfast, they're worth the effort to make at home.

steps.text: Combine flour, sugar, yeast, and salt in a large bowl. Add eggs, milk, lemon zest, and vanilla. Mix until a shaggy dough forms. Knead in softened butter until smooth and elastic, about 10 minutes.
Cover and let rise until doubled, about 1.5 hours.
Roll dough into a large rectangle. Place cold butter block in the center and fold dough over it. Roll out and perform 3 letter folds, chilling 30 minutes between each fold.
Roll dough into a large rectangle about 1/4 inch thick. Cut into 12 triangles.
Roll each triangle from the wide end to the point to form a crescent. Place on parchment-lined baking sheets, curving slightly. Cover and let rise for 45 minutes.
Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Brush cornetti with egg wash.
Bake until deep golden brown, 15-20 minutes. Let cool slightly and dust with powdered sugar.

title: Frittata Primavera
shortDescription: Spring vegetable egg dish with fresh herbs and cheese
note: Finish under the broiler for a golden top
introCopy: This Italian open-faced omelet is endlessly versatile, perfect for using up whatever vegetables you have on hand. Unlike a French omelet, a frittata is cooked slowly over low heat, then finished under the broiler. It's equally good warm or at room temperature, making it ideal for brunch or a light dinner.

steps.text: Preheat broiler. In a large bowl, whisk together eggs, milk, half the Parmigiano, salt, and pepper.
Heat olive oil in a 10-inch oven-safe skillet over medium heat. Add onion and cook until softened, about 5 minutes.
Add zucchini and asparagus. Cook until just tender, about 5 minutes. Add garlic and cherry tomatoes, cook 1 minute more.

Reduce heat to medium-low. Pour egg mixture over vegetables, distributing evenly. Sprinkle with basil and parsley. Cook without stirring until edges are set but center is still slightly runny, about 8 minutes.
Sprinkle remaining Parmigiano over top. Transfer skillet to broiler and cook until top is golden and eggs are fully set, 2-3 minutes. Watch carefully to avoid burning.
Let cool for 5 minutes, then slide onto a serving plate. Cut into wedges and serve warm or at room temperature.
